description: Team Sohan Halwa is a 2-member team from Multan, Pakistan: Daim Ali and Ali Abdullah, computer science students and developers. Our skills include web development, coding, data analysis and visualization. We welcome members interested in astrophysics, data and software.
summary: SkyBlink is a public web tool that shows how a patch of sky changes over time in real NASA SPHEREx survey images. It aligns SPHEREx observations of the same field taken months apart (Data Release 1 and Quick Release 3, one uniformly processed set) on a shared north-up grid with one brightness stretch, and blinks them: moving objects jump, variable stars pulse. The five targets named in the challenge (Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, R Draconis) are pre-loaded with blink explorers, Gaia DR3 and WISE overlays, per-frame quality data, and a spectrum assembled from individual exposures (14 to 74 wavelength channels per target). Pre-loaded targets open instantly; a live search for new fields is available, and it stops with a clear message if the archive does not answer within about 20 seconds. Guided Case Files track interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS across two visits and present a measured proper-motion check on Barnard's Star. The method was validated with 540 synthetic movers injected into real image pairs. No account is needed and nothing is tracked.
details: Planet X, if it exists, is not bright. It is moving, slowly, in images that already exist. SkyBlink starts from that simple idea. It blinks real SPHEREx frames the way Clyde Tombaugh blinked photographic plates to find Pluto, except the plates are now infrared survey data, and the check is stricter: a real mover must move in the same band, in two epochs, and survive a Gaia cross-match. Barnard's Star, the fastest-moving star in our sky, shifts where Gaia predicts, to within a few arcseconds in our frames (1.3 to 7.4 arcseconds across the five epochs, largest where the frame centre sits about a degree away). Comet 3I/ATLAS, only the third interstellar visitor ever seen, moves on a completely different scale. And SkyBlink validated its own pipeline on 540 injected sources before trusting any of it. SkyBlink is a public web tool that shows how a patch of sky changes over time in real NASA SPHEREx survey images. You enter coordinates, or pick one of the pre-loaded targets, and SkyBlink lines up SPHEREx observations of that field taken months apart on a shared north-up grid with one shared brightness stretch, then blinks them. Moving objects jump between frames. Variable stars pulse. Anything that still looks like a discovery is a candidate, not a conclusion: candidates are vetted with the Two-Epoch Check, a vetting method we document and apply in our validation (Methods page and Case File 2). Data and releases. All imagery is SPHEREx Level-2 data from the IRSA archive: Data Release 1 and Quick Release 3, one uniformly processed set. The live backend (https://skyblink-lyart.vercel.app) resolves names through Sesame (CDS) and renders new fields on demand; the search waits about 20 seconds for the archive to answer and then stops with a clear message. The five pre-loaded targets below are served from a prepared cache and open instantly. The five challenge targets. Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis each have a dossier page with a blink explorer (Blink, Side-by-side and Difference views), an ESA Gaia DR3 overlay with proper motions propagated to each frame's date, a WISE (AllWISE) overlay, the clean-pixel percentage and wavelength band of every frame, a detector-band flux chart, and a one-degree context render made from a real survey exposure. Every dossier links the Aladin Lite app, with the SPHEREx all-sky HiPS cube address printed beside it. Every view carries its coordinates in the URL, and the field of view can be set to 3 or 5 arcminutes for live renders. Spectra. Each dossier also shows a spectrum at the target's position, assembled beforehand from individual Level-2 exposures and shipped with the site: Barnard's Star has 74 distinct wavelength channels from 91 exposures (0.80 to 4.89 µm), R Draconis 25 channels, RW Aurigae and WISE 0855 24 each, and Epsilon Indi B 14. Each point's wavelength comes from that frame's own spectral WCS at the target's pixel, and its flux from aperture photometry (radius 2 pixels, annulus background). These are photometric points from aperture photometry, not a calibrated spectrum; faint targets are near the noise, and the zodiacal light model in the archive products is not subtracted from Level-2 data. Case Files. Three guided cases use real data end to end. Case 1 follows interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS between its 13 August and 14 December 2025 visits, two positions 79.2 degrees apart. Case 2 documents the Two-Epoch Check. Case 3 measures Barnard's Star: centroided in all five epochs, its positions agree with Gaia's proper-motion prediction to within 1.3 to 7.4 arcseconds. The two largest offsets come from the two frames centred about a degree away from the star; with five frames, detector, position and band effects cannot be separated, so the pattern is reported as a hypothesis, not a finding. The case data can be downloaded as CSV. Validation. We injected 540 synthetic moving objects (Gaussian sources) into real epoch pairs and ran the site's own difference test on them. Recovery was 100 percent at signal levels of 15 sigma and above, and 97 to 98 percent at 8 sigma for shifts of 2 pixels or more. A control run on uninjected pairs found 439 raw residual peaks at 6 sigma and above, which is the measured reason a candidate still has to pass the Two-Epoch Check. Injected sources are idealised Gaussians tested with our own rule; this measures the sensitivity of the difference test, not performance on real movers. Access and maintenance. The explorer is fully keyboard-operable, the difference palette is colour-blind-safe, the site ships in dark and light themes, and it runs on phones with no account and no tracking. A weekly job checks the archive for new epochs of the five targets and refreshes the cache when the survey revisits them. The site is a static front end with a FastAPI backend; the full source is at https://github.com/Daimx1214/skyblink AI use. We used AI assistants for research, planning, drafting code and writing, under the team's direction. All data shown are real archive products; nothing is simulated. Team Sohan Halwa: Daim Ali and Ali Abdullah, Universal Event.
